title: Talmadge's piano and drum lessons
summary: Talmadge started on piano, then drums with Lenny Rosenthal, but lost interest when his teacher changed.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: That's great. What year was it that Talmadge was born?
'36. The next year after I came to California.
And you mentioned on the tape that had to be re-recorded, so we don't have it on here, that you -- he was originally interested in music and he took music lessons?
Well, he started on piano. I wanted so badly, I suppose like most people in music, you know. I

don't -- you know, I don't say that I would have wanted him to be a professional musician, you know. That would be up to him to choose this, and I think this is the way it should be with any child. I don't think you should just force it on him. But I was hoping that he would have been musical, you know, would have liked music enough to stick with it. And he loved it, and he still does, you know. And he could get to the piano and he would pick out little things on the piano, you know, and I was so thrilled. I said, "Well, maybe he's going to play the piano." And I had him under -- oh, at different times, two or three different teachers at different times. Wonderful teachers. Marvelous. Very good with kids and beginners, you know. But he would do all right as long as he was with them, but he would never practice. He didn't like it well enough to practice. So they all said the same thing. They all advised me to stop him until he really showed interest. So this is what I did and he never did really show interest.

Later he said to me, he said, "Mother, you know what I would like to do? I would like to study the drums." Well, Sid Catlett was a friend of mine and a very marvelous musician, and he said, "I think I would like to play the drums." I said, "Do you really?" He said, "Yes, that's what I would like. I want to be a drummer like Sid." I said, "Well, that's wonderful." So naturally I was thrilled over that. And I got a good teacher for him and got him some drums, you know, and he did very well.
He did very, very, very well. And as a matter of fact he studied for about four years at Fine Arts Conservatory.

The young fellow that was teaching him had never travelled, you know, with a big band, and he wanted to travel. I think his name was Rosenthal, Lenny Rosenthal. And he wanted to travel, you know. But he was so marvelous with my son, and my son just adored him and he adored my son, and he did just very, very, very, very well. And then he used to call and tell me, you know, when I'd come to town. I travelled quite a bit at that time, but I had a housekeeper that used to, you know, keep me informed, and I'd call home sometimes two, three times a week, talking to Talmadge, you know, to see how he was getting along. And then my sister and her husband lived right next door in one of the apartments, and they looked after the place for me and helped with Talmadge, and this housekeeper kept me aware of everything. And he was practicing. Oh, he did practice. He loved the drums.

But when Lenny decided that he no longer was going to teach, you know, he was going to give it up for awhile, and he had all of his students assigned to someone else. And my son said to me -- his first assignment with this teacher, he didn't like him. He'd made up his mind he wasn't going to like him. And so he said to me, "I don't care much for that teacher, mother." I said, "Well, listen, you're not supposed to be in love with the teacher. The teacher's there to teach you. This

is for your good. He's a good teacher and he knows what he's doing. He's experienced." But I knew what the problem was. He was an older man, you know, and he probably didn't kid around with him and play with him. He was very sincere and -- I don't mean the other guy wasn't. The other guy was very good, but he was a younger teacher, and I think that made the difference.

However, he did not ever do anything with the drums, so I talked with the teacher and I told him. I said, "Well, what do you think?" He said, "Well, I would advise you to -- let's stop him." He said, "Let's stop him and see. Maybe later on he'll go back to it. But right now he's not doing anything. He doesn't show any interest." And I said, "Well, I don't want him wasting money and time, because he's wasting my money and your time."
